observed_through_basis: https://www.wjhg.com/content/news/Calhoun-County-Hurricane-Michael-recovery-updates-498266401.html - 'Calhoun Liberty Hospital is on generator power with an open Emergency Department.'
notes: THE SINGLE CITED SOURCE IS INADEQUATE AND PARTLY MISLEADING AS USED. The registry's only citation is the hospital's own retrospective marketing page, whose 'never closed its doors' claim is, on the contemporaneous record, true only of the EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT. I located three independent sources the row does not cite, and they materially complicate the SIP_OK label. WHAT IS NOW SUPPORTED: the hospital did not evacuate before landfall and was still functioning on site afterward - WJHG's Calhoun County status report (published Oct. 22, 2018; hospital line carried in the Oct. 24, 2018 update) states it was 'on generator power with an open Emergency Department', and its damage narrative (roof torn off, windows smashed, ongoing water intrusion) is only consistent with the building being occupied and operating through the storm. That supports the 'sheltered' half of SIP_OK, though no source describes the facility's status on Oct 10 itself, so I grade it partial rather than yes. WHAT IS NOT SUPPORTED - AND THIS IS THE REASON I RECOMMEND REVIEW: SIP_OK requires the hospital to be 'documented as operating without forced patient movement', and no source documents that. The opposite-leaning evidence is affirmative and from two independent outlets. WJHG (Nov. 16, 2018): 'The storm tore off the hospital's roof, smashed windows, and while the emergency room remains open, the hospital remains closed to inpatients with no reopening in sight', and 'Patients needing hospital care in the Blountstown area are being sent to Dothan or Tallahassee.' Tallahassee Democrat (Jul. 19, 2019): 'It wasn't until this spring that the hospital reopened inpatient services', with '80 percent of its roof ... peeled away' and the main lobby and lab 'forced to close and relocate'; bed count fell from 25 to 10. So this 25-bed critical access hospital's inpatient unit ceased functioning at the storm and stayed shut for roughly five to six months. If ANY inpatients were on census when Michael struck on Oct 10, 2018, they necessarily had to be moved out afterward - which is precisely the POST_FSIP pattern (sheltered, then patients forced out because operations broke down). No source I could reach states the Oct 10-11 inpatient census or what became of those patients; the Tallahassee Democrat feature, which is the most detailed retrospective available, describes the storm damage at length and never mentions an evacuation or transfer either way. RECOMMENDED RESOLUTION: do not keep this row as a clean SIP_OK on the current basis. Obtain the Oct 10, 2018 inpatient census / discharge-transfer records (Florida AHCA emergency status reporting, the hospital's own CMS cost report or Medicare claims for transfers dated Oct 10-15, 2018, or a direct statement from hospital administration). If the census was zero at landfall (plausible for a 25-bed CAH that had days of warning and may have discharged down), SIP_OK is defensible but should be re-cited to the WJHG Oct 2018 status report rather than the hospital's About page, and the detail field should be corrected to say the ED stayed open while inpatient services were lost. If any inpatients were transferred out post-landfall, relabel to POST_FSIP with evac_start on or about 2018-10-10/11. Either way the current LOW confidence should stand or drop until that is settled. CAVEAT ON observed_through: I set it to 2018-10-24, the latest date on which a source shows the facility operating on site. Be aware this is ED-only operation; it is not evidence that no inpatient transfer occurred, and it should not be read as such in the paper. LATER FORCED EVACUATION: none found. The facility limped on and was ultimately replaced - FEMA approved roughly $11.4 million in 2020 and a new $47 million hospital opened in July/August 2025 - but that is a rebuild, not a storm evacuation.

(b) The detail-field claim that 'some local nursing home patients used the hospital as refuge' is NOT in either fetched source and should be re-sourced or deleted. Corroboration is thinner than ideal: the only post-landfall source is a responding NGO's self-published operational blog rather than news or official reporting, and independent verification was constrained this session (WebSearch quota exhausted, web.archive.org unreachable via the fetch tool, DuckDuckGo/Mojeek CAPTCHA/403). observed_through_basis: https://www.propublica.org/article/in-hurricanes-wake-decisions-not-to-evacuate-hospitals-raise-questions — "backup power kept functioning at all of North Shore-LIJ's hospitals"
notes: All three cited URLs are live. The abcnews.go.com form of the URL 301-redirects to abcnews.com (the form cited in the CSV), which fetched fine — no Wayback needed. Evidence is strong that Southside did not undergo a full or post-landfall evacuation: ABC News on 2012-10-29 (pre-landfall) reports the 16 North Shore-LIJ hospitals would remain open; ProPublica (2012-11-01), an article specifically about hospitals that chose NOT to evacuate, names NYU Langone, Bellevue and Coney Island as the facilities that evacuated and states backup power held at all North Shore-LIJ hospitals, which instead ACCEPTED 158 transfers by Wednesday night. TWO QUALIFICATIONS the authors should carry into the paper. (1) Partial pre-storm evacuation: this was not a pure shelter-in-place. Both the Columbia/Sandy case study ('Lesser of Two Evils: Evacuate or Stay? observed_through_basis: https://web.archive.org/web/20170911165314/http://www.thedenverchannel.com/news/local-news/coloradans-helping-florida-hospitals-respond-to-irma — "Smedberg has taken over the safety and security operations at the hospital."
notes:
SOURCE CHAIN. The single cited URL is a Florida Trend health-care news roundup (dated 9/12/2017), not a reported article. Its entire Broward Health North content is a two-sentence aggregator blurb of a Denver7 (KMGH) story: "Downed trees, heavy winds and torrential rain are among the images capturing a glimpse of Irma passing over Broward Health North hospital in Florida. Denver native Matthew Smedberg has been calling the hospital home." The live page still carries this text; I also pulled the 2017-09-24 Wayback capture and the text is identical, so the cited source is intact (no link rot). I traced and retrieved the underlying Denver7 article from the Wayback Machine (capture 2017-09-11 16:53 GMT; byline timestamp 7:53 AM, Sep 11, 2017) and record it as additional_source.

WHAT THE SOURCES ACTUALLY SHOW. The Denver7 piece is an interview with Matthew Smedberg, an HSS Security contractor from Denver who was training staff at Broward Health North and rode out the storm there, taking over the hospital's safety and security operations. It establishes: (i) the hospital went into lockdown the morning of Sep 10 and was occupied and staffed while Irma passed over — i.e., no pre-landfall closure/relocation of operations; (ii) no evacuation or patient transfer is mentioned anywhere; (iii) the hospital lost utility power when the hurricane hit; and (iv) there were "a couple of little fires" inside the hospital from water intrusion and electrical damage. The Florida Trend blurb adds nothing beyond the first sentence.

WHY ONLY 'PARTIAL' ON sheltered_supported. Skeptically read, neither source ever mentions patients, census, admissions, or operating status. They document staff/security presence and building conditions during the storm, not that inpatients remained in the building or that the hospital continued clinical operations. A facility that had moved patients out pre-landfall could equally have had a ride-out security team on site. So the absence of a pre-landfall evacuation is strongly implied (hospital in hurricane lockdown, contractor sheltering inside, storm passing over) but is nowhere stated, and 'stayed open' is not stated by any source at all.

REGISTRY DETAIL OVER-READS THE SOURCE. The abstracted detail says "Sheltered in place and stayed open through heavy winds, downed trees and torrential rain." The "downed trees, heavy winds and torrential rain" clause is lifted from the blurb, but "stayed open" is an inference not supported by the cited text. Recommend softening the detail field to what the source supports (occupied and in lockdown through the storm) or citing the Denver7 original directly.

ADVERSE SIGNAL WORTH RECORDING. The Denver7 story documents loss of utility power at the hospital during Irma plus water intrusion causing small internal electrical fires. That is real infrastructure degradation of exactly the kind that drives POST_FSIP events elsewhere in the registry. It does not by itself defeat SIP_OK — there is no evidence of any forced patient movement, and generator backup is the expected response — but it means this facility was not an undisturbed shelter-in-place, and the coding rests on absence of evidence of transfer rather than on positive documentation of uninterrupted operation.

SEARCH FOR A LATER FORCED EVACUATION. I found none. WebSearch was unavailable (session search budget exhausted, 200/200) and Bing/DuckDuckGo/Brave/Ecosia/Mojeek all returned bot-detection or CAPTCHA pages, which I did not attempt to bypass. I substituted Google News RSS queries ("Broward Health North" Irma; "Broward Health" hurricane Irma evacuate; Broward hospitals Irma date-bounded 2017-09-10 to 2017-09-20) and the Wayback CDX API. Nothing surfaced any Broward Health North evacuation or patient transfer. The prominent post-Irma South Florida forced-movement story in those results is the Rehabilitation Center at Hollywood Hills nursing home (patients moved to Memorial Regional Hospital) — a different, non-Broward Health facility, so it is not a contradiction here. The Wayback capture of browardhealth.org from 2017-09-13 shows a stale homepage with no Irma status statement and is recorded only to document that this avenue was checked.

BOTTOM LINE. SIP_OK is the most plausible label and nothing contradicts it, but the evidence base is one two-sentence aggregator blurb plus its underlying human-interest TV story that never mentions patients. observed_through is set to 2017-09-11 (the Denver7 publication date, the day after Irma's Broward-area conditions), which is the last date on which a source shows the hospital occupied and running its own operations with no transfer reported. Keep at reduced confidence (the row's MEDIUM confidence is, if anything, generous), and ideally add a corroborating source that positively documents patients/operations — e.g., a Broward Health or AHCA post-Irma facility-status statement, or Sun Sentinel/WPLG/NBC6 coverage of which Broward hospitals remained open — before this event carries weight in the analysis.

That establishes the hospital was staffed and functioning on generator power on landfall day, which is inconsistent with a pre-landfall evacuation, but NO source states explicitly that patients were not evacuated, and there is no post-storm source confirming continued operation after July 10. Source quality is a concern for a peer-reviewed citation: Wikinews is a user-generated wiki and is the sole citation. Extensive searching (Pensacola News Journal-type coverage, Pensapedia's Hurricane Dennis entry, CHA/Catholic Health World, ASPR TRACIE, Navy/globalsecurity items) found no independent contemporaneous account of Sacred Heart Pensacola during Dennis; globalsecurity.org returned 403 and web.archive.org is unreachable from this environment (both WebFetch and curl fail to connect), so no Wayback verification was possible. No evidence of any evacuation or closure of Sacred Heart during Dennis or its aftermath was found, so the SIP_OK direction is not contradicted — but the evidentiary basis is thin (single wiki source, single landfall-day data point). Recommend keeping the record at lowered confidence and, if possible, adding a durable citation (e.g., Pensacola News Journal July 2005 archive or Florida AHCA/ESF-8 facility status reports).

observed_through_basis: https://wcti12.com/news/local/fema-approves-nearly-17-million-to-repair-onslow-memorial-hospital — "The hospital has been operating without a fully operational roof since the September storm hit."
notes: Source 1 (Advisory Board Daily Briefing, Sept 17, 2018) is live and supports the abstracted phone-outage detail — it reports NCHA said Onslow Memorial and Moore Regional lost inbound/outbound phone service from storm damage. It lists which hospitals evacuated/reopened (Bladen, Tidelands, Grand Strand, etc.) and Onslow Memorial is NOT among the evacuated; it is described only as a damaged but functioning facility. That is supportive by omission, not an explicit statement. Source 2 (WNCT) returns HTTP 403 from a HUMAN Security bot wall on the canonical URL; the /amp/ variant of the same article fetched successfully and confirms the education-building detail (out of service two years). Wayback could not be used — web.archive.org is unreachable from this environment via both WebFetch and curl (connection refused / 429), so no wayback-status entries could be produced. NO source located states in so many words that Onslow Memorial did not evacuate patients; the strongest continuity evidence is WCTI-12 (Apr 17, 2019), which reports the hospital 'has been operating' continuously since the September storm while awaiting a new roof, plus FEMA's ~$1.7M Public Assistance award for repairs. Targeted searches for a later forced evacuation, closure, or patient transfer at Onslow Memorial during Florence's aftermath (including the county's own Florence response/recovery report and NC DOA repair notices) found none — the record is not contradicted. Recommend keeping at lowered confidence and adding the WCTI-12 (2019-04-17) post-storm continuity citation and, ideally, a September 2018 primary statement from the hospital or NCHA.

observed_through_basis: https://wpde.com/news/local/an-update-on-robeson-county-after-hurricane-florence — "All Southeastern Regional Medical Centers in Robeson County, except Maxton Clinic, are open"
notes: Important sourcing gap in the row as cited: the single cited URL (NC Health News, Sept 12, 2018) is live and supports every abstracted detail — the $3.5M generator investment, the Matthew-2016 water/communications loss, and the lobby space offered to oxygen-dependent residents with continuous power — but it is PRE-LANDFALL and documents intent, not outcome. It cannot by itself establish SIP_OK. Two post-landfall sources found in this audit close that gap. NC Health News (Sept 18, 2018) quotes Southeastern Health's David Sumner, interviewed Sunday Sept 16 (two days after landfall), saying the flagship hospital in Lumberton was on diversion — i.e., open and staffed, taking no NEW patients and diverting incoming emergencies, with community members on home oxygen showing up for help during the storm (fewer than during Matthew). Diversion is a load-shedding posture, not an evacuation, and no transfer of admitted inpatients is reported. WPDE (Sept 20, 2018, after the Lumber River crest of ~25.4 ft) reports all Southeastern Regional facilities in Robeson County except the Maxton Clinic open under normal business hours; other coverage notes the hospital trucked in water after the municipal plant flooded. Searches for a later forced evacuation, closure, or patient transfer at Southeastern Regional during Florence's aftermath found none; the hospital's Matthew-era vulnerabilities (water, generators) recurred but were managed in place. Keep the SIP_OK label, but the authors should add the Sept 18 NC Health News and Sept 20 WPDE citations so the record rests on post-landfall evidence, and may wish to note the Sept 16 ED-diversion status as a service-degradation nuance. web.archive.org was unreachable from this environment, but no source required it.

observed_through_basis: https://theshift.usacs.com/when-this-disaster-happened-we-were-there/ — "On Sunday, the staffing plan called for team C to come relieve" (Sunday = 2018-09-16; teams A/B had staffed the hospital continuously Thursday–Saturday, Sept 13–15). Corroborating but not directly fetchable (HTTP 403): ASHP News, 2018-09-17, search-engine snippet describing pharmacy staff sleeping on cots at "the 301-bed hospital, which remains on lockdown" as of Monday.
notes: The single cited source (Global News, 2018-09-17, by Josh K. Elliott) was fetched twice with keyword searches for hospital/CarolinaEast/medical center/helicopter/CEO/Leggett: none appear. It documents New Bern flooding and rescues only and does not support any hospital-specific claim; it should be replaced. The abstracted 'CEO described contingency plans including helicopter resupply' detail traces (per search snippets) to Modern Healthcare's 2018-09-11 pre-storm article quoting CarolinaEast Health System CEO Raymond Leggett, not to Global News; that article and its pressreader reprint returned HTTP 403 and Wayback was unreachable from this environment (WebFetch cannot access web.archive.org; curl from the sandbox got no connection / HTTP 429 on the availability API). The SIP_OK label itself IS supported by the USACS account (fetched): the hospital, built to Category 5 standards, stayed open with ED teams living on site Thursday through Sunday, took in patients transferred by first responders and community oxygen/dialysis-dependent people who sheltered in recliners in the PT area; only non-essential PROVIDERS were allowed to evacuate west the night before, not patients. No source found reporting any patient evacuation or closure of CarolinaEast during or after Florence. Minor discrepancy: abstraction says 350-bed; ASHP snippet says 301-bed. Recommend keeping SIP_OK but swapping the citation to USACS (+ASHP/Modern Healthcare) and treating confidence as MEDIUM-LOW until an author can open the 403-blocked ASHP/Modern Healthcare pages. WebSearch budget was exhausted at the end of this audit, so no further alternative sources could be sought.

observed_through_basis: https://www.advisory.com/daily-briefing/2018/09/17/florence (2018-09-17) — NHRMC "unable to receive inbound calls" and launched a temporary line, i.e., operating on 9/17; retrospective hospital-side account https://strengthenhealthcare.org/a-port-in-the-storm/ (2019-01-07): "the hospital remained open 24/7" during the week Florence devastated Wilmington.
notes: All four cited URLs fetched. Strengthen Healthcare (2019-01-07; hospital-side retrospective) directly supports shelter-in-place: 1,800 staff sheltered in on 9/12, 500 patients cared for and 42 babies delivered on generator power, ceiling leaks repaired, medical shelters set up at nearby schools, eight NICU babies transferred out BEFORE the storm to WakeMed/UNC/Levine. Scientific American (2018-09-13) and NC Health News (2018-09-12) are pre-landfall and only partially support: they confirm the main hospital intended to ride out the storm and document the 9/12 closures of Pender Memorial, NHRMC Orthopedic Hospital and the Scotts Hill ED (matching the abstracted detail). Gov1 (page shows 2019-12-26 but is a reprint of an AP wire story from 2018-09-16/17) confirms Wilmington was cut off and contains one line the authors should be aware of: on Sunday 9/16 'patients on oxygen and dialysis were being moved from New Hanover County Medical Center to Hoggard High School,' a newly opened 1,387-capacity shelter. Read together with the hospital's own account of 'setting up medical shelters at nearby schools' and HCI's report of a medical shelter at a school for displaced residents needing specialized care, this reads as decompression of medically dependent community shelterees (not admitted inpatients) into a hospital-run medical shelter, not a forced evacuation of the hospital; no source describes any post-landfall evacuation or closure of the main campus, and Advisory.com (9/17) shows it operating (phone outage, temporary line). Pre-storm movements (some ambulatory patients on 9/11 per WECT; 8 NICU infants) were voluntary decompression before landfall and are already acknowledged in the abstraction. Later NC AHEC update notes flooding of NHRMC/SEAHEC residency offices, library and labs, but no interruption of clinical operations. Label SIP_OK supported; HIGH confidence is reasonable. Suggest adding the Hoggard High School caveat to the record notes.

hospital: MUSC Medical Center (Medical University of South Carolina)
observed_through_basis: http://www.live5news.com/2018/09/21/musc-helping-patients-affected-by-hurricane-florence/ (2018-09-21) — "MUSC was prepared for whatever the storm could bring and stayed open throughout the week"; MUSC was receiving (~50) transfer patients from Horry County, not sending them.
notes: The single cited source (Advisory Board Daily Briefing, 2018-09-17) was fetched and confirms the abstracted timing exactly: MUSC in Charleston 'resumed normal operations on Monday' (9/17), listed alongside East Cooper, Roper St. Francis, Trident/Summerville and Tenet hospitals; it does not itself state that MUSC stayed open during the storm, hence 'partial'. The shelter-in-place claim is independently supported by Live 5 News (fetched, 2018-09-21): MUSC 'stayed open throughout the week', received about 50 transfer patients (mostly from Horry County; many to ICU) plus displaced dialysis patients, and ran free telehealth for ~150 people — i.e., MUSC functioned as a receiving hospital under the coastal mandatory evacuation (Charleston County was under Gov. McMaster's 9/11 evacuation order; hospitals were exempt per search snippets of the CNN 9/12 story, which returned HTTP 451 and could not be fetched). Pre-storm Live 5 coverage (9/10-11) shows the plan was to remain open with a 7-day stockpile and staff sleeping on site; outpatient clinics closed and electives were cancelled from Wednesday 9/12. The MUSC Catalyst News item 'Tallying up Florence's impact on MUSC Health' (2018-09-17) now redirects to the MUSC homepage (dead) and Wayback was unreachable from this environment. No source found indicating any evacuation or closure of MUSC Medical Center during or after Florence (Florence was only a tropical storm in Charleston, 9/14-15). SIP_OK supported; recommend adding the Live 5 News 9/21 article as a second citation.

observed_through_basis: https://www.advisory.com/daily-briefing/2018/09/17/florence — "resuming normal operations on Monday include: ... Roper St. Francis Healthcare in Charleston"
notes: Both cited URLs are live and both directly support the SIP_OK label. Weather.com (dated 2018-09-15, i.e. after the 2018-09-14 landfall) states Roper Hospital remained open, with only express care and physician-partner offices closed because they did not meet the state shelter-in-place requirement — exactly matching the CSV 'detail' field. Advisory Board (2018-09-17) lists Roper St. Francis Healthcare among South Carolina facilities resuming normal operations on Monday, which is 2018-09-17. I added an official state source not in the CSV: the SC Department of Environmental Services (formerly DHEC) Hurricane Florence update of 2018-09-13, which lists the 7 hospitals that closed under the Governor's 2018-09-10 Mandatory Medical Evacuation order and the 8 granted exemptions 'allowing them to continue to treat their most acutely ill patients'; Roper Hospital and Bon Secours-St. Francis Xavier (Roper) both appear on the exemption list, and Roper appears on neither closure nor evacuation list. Searched specifically for any later Florence-related evacuation, closure or patient transfer at Roper (WebSearch on hospital name plus Florence plus evacuate/closed) and found none; Charleston was on the storm's southern periphery and the Advisory Board roundup places Roper back to normal operations. No contradicting evidence. The CSV records confidence MEDIUM; the state exemption list plus two post-landfall trade sources would justify raising it to HIGH.

observed_through_basis: https://www.advisory.com/daily-briefing/2018/09/17/florence — "Other South Carolina-based facilities resuming normal operations on Monday include: East Cooper Medical Center"
notes: Both cited URLs are live and support the label. Note a naming variance: weather.com calls the facility 'East Cooper Regional Medical Center' while the CSV, the Advisory Board piece and the SC state list all use 'East Cooper Medical Center'; these are the same Mount Pleasant, SC facility (CCN 420089) and the variance is not a mismatch. Advisory Board (2018-09-17) names East Cooper Medical Center as resuming normal operations Monday, giving observed_through 2018-09-17. Added official corroboration not in the CSV: the SC DES Hurricane Florence update of 2018-09-13 names East Cooper Medical Center among the 8 hospitals granted exemptions to the Governor's Mandatory Medical Evacuation order, i.e. the state affirmatively authorized it to shelter in place and keep treating patients; it is absent from the list of 7 hospitals reported closed. observed_through_basis: https://www.hfmmagazine.com/articles/211-a-hospital-reborn — "which was not powered by emergency generators, to be out of service for several days" (date derived, not stated)
notes: The single cited source (HFM Magazine, live) does NOT by itself state that Woman's Hospital sheltered in place or stayed open. It only says Gustav damaged the substations serving the hospital and that the AC, not on emergency power, was out for several days, and that this drove the 3x2MW (6 MW) generator design in the replacement facility — so on the cited source alone this row would be only partly supported. I therefore added two sources. (1) The hospital's own 2008 Annual Report (womans.org PDF; text extracted with pdftotext) documents that Woman's was a point of refuge during Gustav, cared for 45 evacuated infants from southeast Louisiana plus 22 adult patients, that 17 of those infants were born at Woman's, and captions a photo of a nurse overseeing 'the return of an infant evacuated before the storm' — an inbound-receiving, not outbound-evacuating, role, with no mention anywhere of evacuating its own patients. (2) CNN, 2008-08-31 (live URL blocked with HTTP 451; retrieved via Wayback), names Woman's Hospital in Baton Rouge as the NICU receiving hospital for East Jefferson General and Touro Infirmary and reports it holding 32 evacuated babies by Sunday evening, i.e. the night before the 2008-09-01 landfall. Together these establish that the hospital did not evacuate before landfall and kept operating. CAVEAT the authors should note: observed_through 2008-09-04 is DERIVED, not quoted. No source gives a calendar date after landfall for Woman's; 2008-09-04 is the conservative reading of 'several days' after the 2008-09-01 landfall during which the hospital was occupied without AC. If the authors want only source-stated dates, observed_through should be 2008-09-01 (CNN, night before landfall). RESIDUAL RISK checked but not resolved: post-Gustav, Louisiana officials estimated almost 700 patients in a dozen unnamed hospitals might need evacuation specifically because generators could not run air conditioning (nbcnews.com/id/wbna26517000, 2008-09-03), and Woman's was AC-less for several days, so it plausibly sat in that at-risk group. I searched for evidence that Woman's was among them and found none: ProPublica's two Gustav hospital pieces name only Earl K. Long (fully evacuated) and Lane Regional Medical Center (generator failure, critical patients moved) and never mention Woman's, and the hospital's own annual report, which describes its Gustav role in detail, records no outbound transfer. No contradicting evidence found, so keep SIP_OK; the CSV's MEDIUM confidence remains appropriate and should not be raised, because the absence of a named post-landfall status report for Woman's is an evidentiary gap rather than positive confirmation.

observed_through_basis: https://web.archive.org/web/20191021073207/https://www.reliasmedia.com/articles/1140-pensacola-hospital-and-patients-survive-battering-by-hurricane-ivan — "postponed elective surgery until the following Wednesday, Sept. 22"
notes: Primary cited source is alive only by redirect: reliasmedia.com 301s to clinician.com, which returns HTTP 403 to automated fetch; full text recovered from the Wayback capture 20191021073207. The article (AHC Media, published 2004-12-01, based on interviews with social services manager Susan Kearney and PR manager Mike Burke) is a detailed facility-level account and independently confirms every element of the abstracted narrative: ~2 a.m. Sept. 16 landfall, ~130 mph winds on boarded-up windows, loss of utility power and operation on emergency generators, staff pre-positioned before landfall anticipating transportation problems, and more than 2,000 family members sheltered in the hospital. It explicitly describes continuous operation through and after the storm ("We delivered babies, did heart catheterization, and emergency surgery"), minor non-structural damage, elective surgery resuming Wed. Sept. 22, ED volume up 40% over the two weeks after the storm, and a FEMA DMAT setting up tents outside the ED — i.e. the hospital was a receiving, not a sending, facility. No evacuation or patient transfer out of the facility is mentioned anywhere. The intra-facility movement of all 360 patients into interior hallways and of lobby visitors to the basement is a within-building protective action, not a forced transfer, and does not undercut SIP_OK. Targeted searches for any later forced evacuation or closure of Sacred Heart Pensacola during the Ivan aftermath returned nothing; the record instead shows normal/expanded operations through at least end of September 2004. observed_through is set conservatively to 2004-09-22 (the explicitly dated resumption of elective surgery); the same article supports operation through roughly 2004-09-30 via the 'two weeks after the storm' ED-volume statement. The second cited source (WUWF) is a 10-year retrospective, not contemporaneous, and only records Gov. Jeb Bush reporting damage to Pensacola hospitals including Sacred Heart; it corroborates storm impact and timing but says nothing about evacuation status, so it does not by itself support the label. Note a minor internal inconsistency in that source: its URL/publication date is 2014-09-16 but its headline reads '14 Years Later'; this does not affect the finding. Confidence HIGH in the CSV is appropriate.

observed_through_basis: https://web.archive.org/web/20041026111844/http://www.ebaptisthealthcare.org/BHC/NewsEvents/Default.aspx?ContentID=100877 — "Jay Hospital, Atmore Community Hospital and D.W. McMillan Memorial Hospital also continued to operate."
notes: The single cited source (ebaptisthealthcare.org/about/history) is live and does carry the system-level claim, but it is an undated corporate timeline page written years after the fact, so on its own it justifies only the CSV's LOW confidence. The audit recovered a contemporaneous, facility-named replacement: the Baptist Health Care press release 'Baptist Health Care Facilities Are Up and Running,' preserved in the Wayback Machine and linked from the BHC homepage capture of 2004-09-25 (web.archive.org/web/20040925122701/http://www.bhcpns.org/). The release is internally dated 'one week after Hurricane Ivan' (i.e. ~2004-09-23) and names Jay Hospital explicitly as having continued to operate, within a statement that 'All five Baptist Health Care hospitals remained in operation during Hurricane Ivan and its aftermath.' Importantly, this release is not a blanket PR claim: it enumerates the two BHC facilities that were closed (Baptist Medical Park-Navarre, still being assessed, and West Side Rehab Clinic) and itemizes damaged/suspended services at Baptist Hospital (fourth-floor acute dialysis and MICU relocated within the building, SurgiCare, Cardiopulmonary Rehab Center), which makes the affirmative statement about Jay Hospital substantially more credible than a generic assurance. This upgrades the evidence from system-level to facility-specific and contemporaneous; the CSV detail field's caveat 'No facility-specific account recovered' is now out of date and should be revised. Remaining limitation: all supporting text is self-reported by the operating health system; no independent third-party (news, state agency, peer-reviewed) confirmation of Jay Hospital's individual storm-time status was located despite targeted searches. Searches for any later forced evacuation, patient transfer, or closure of Jay Hospital during the Ivan aftermath found nothing contradicting SIP_OK. Jay Hospital is inland in northern Santa Rosa County, away from the surge zone, which is consistent with a ride-out. Suggest keeping SIP_OK and considering raising confidence from LOW to MODERATE, with the source citation updated to the archived 2004 press release.

observed_through_basis: https://web.archive.org/web/20041026111844/http://www.ebaptisthealthcare.org/BHC/NewsEvents/Default.aspx?ContentID=100877 — "This includes Baptist Hospital and Gulf Breeze Hospitals, both of which are located"
notes: Same evidentiary upgrade as E072. The only cited source is the live but undated ebaptisthealthcare.org history timeline, carrying a system-level claim. The audit recovered the contemporaneous Baptist Health Care press release 'Baptist Health Care Facilities Are Up and Running' (Wayback; linked from the BHC homepage capture of 2004-09-25, internally dated 'one week after Hurricane Ivan,' i.e. ~2004-09-23), which names Gulf Breeze Hospital explicitly and, notably, flags it as one of the two BHC hospitals 'located in hard-hit areas' that nonetheless remained in operation during Ivan and its aftermath. This directly addresses the CSV's stated concern that Gulf Breeze sits on the peninsula between Pensacola Bay and Santa Rosa Sound in the surge zone. The release's credibility is strengthened by its explicit enumeration of the BHC facilities that were closed (Baptist Medical Park-Navarre; West Side Rehab Clinic) and of damaged services at Baptist Hospital, so it is not an undifferentiated 'everything is fine' statement. The CSV detail field's caveat 'No facility-specific account recovered' should be revised. Limitations: the evidence remains self-reported by the operating health system; no independent contemporaneous news, state (AHCA/FL DOH), or federal source specific to Gulf Breeze Hospital's storm-time status was located despite targeted searching, and Pensacola News Journal archives from September 2004 were not reachable. Actively searched for a later forced evacuation, patient transfer, or closure of Gulf Breeze Hospital in the Ivan aftermath — including scenarios arising from the destruction of the Escambia Bay I-10 bridge and damage to peninsula road access — and found no evidence of any; the archived press release affirmatively covers the aftermath period through ~Sept 23. Nothing contradicts SIP_OK. Suggest keeping SIP_OK and considering raising confidence from LOW to MODERATE, with the citation updated to the archived 2004 press release.

observed_through_basis: https://memorialhermann.org/about-us/newsroom/press-releases/update-on-memorial-hermann-hospitals-after-hurricane-ike — "Memorial Hermann-Texas Medical Center and Memorial Hermann Katy Hospital remain on regular power" (system update dated Sept 13, 2008, i.e. after Ike's ~2:10 a.m. CDT Sept 13 landfall).
notes: Both cited URLs are live. Wikipedia is hospital-specific and post-landfall: it places Memorial Hermann receiving walk-in patients and says the Texas Medical Center campus kept its lights on while the region was dark — consistent with SIP_OK, though Wikipedia is a tertiary source and its own citation was not separately verified. The PMC source (Bull World Health Organ, Nov 2009) does NOT name Memorial Hermann; it documents the TMC-wide post-Ike water-pressure episode and, by its own wording ('almost resulted'), confirms the near-mass-evacuation was averted. Because that source is campus-aggregate, I added the Memorial Hermann Health System's own Sept 13, 2008 update as a hospital-specific, post-landfall anchor; it states MH-TMC stayed on utility power and identifies the ONLY system hospital that evacuated as Memorial Hermann Southeast Hospital, a separate facility with a different CCN. Two caveats the authors should carry: (1) the strongest hospital-specific documentation stops at Sept 13, while the TMC water-pressure crisis peaked roughly Sept 14-16, so no dated source directly certifies MH-TMC's inpatient census went untouched during those days — the averted-evacuation evidence for that window is aggregate, not facility-level; (2) there is a real abstraction hazard between Memorial Hermann-TMC (sheltered) and Memorial Hermann Southeast (evacuated Sept 11 and closed) — confirm the CCN mapping is 450068. I searched for any later Ike-aftermath forced evacuation or closure of MH-TMC and found none. Rice University's Sept 25, 2008 piece corroborates that TMC came 'extremely close' to a flood emergency that did not materialize.

observed_through_basis: https://www.coastalpoint.com/news/communities/dagsboro/breaking-news-area-begins-recovery-from-hurricane-irene-with-mostly-minor-damage-reported/article_2cd0cb0f-fb3d-55c1-b199-fe4e389841db.html — "remained fully staffed and ready for traumas and other emergency situations throughout the storm" (article published Aug 28, 2011, after Irene cleared coastal Delaware).
notes: The single cited URL is live and is a good source for this label: it is contemporaneous local news dated Aug 28, 2011 — after Irene passed over Sussex County overnight Aug 27-28 — it names Beebe's Lewes main campus on Savannah Road specifically, describes the ED, ORs and Labor and Delivery as staffed and operating in the past tense 'throughout the storm', and reports that inpatient and most outpatient services on the main campus would resume as of Monday, Aug 29. Resumption of inpatient service implies inpatients were retained rather than transferred out. Two reasons for lower confidence rather than plain 'keep': (1) the record rests on ONE local outlet — I ran multiple searches (Cape Gazette, Delaware Public Media, WHYY, Sussex County government, Delaware DHSS, Beebe's own press archive, CBS Philadelphia) and found no independent source that names Beebe in connection with Irene, so there is no corroboration and no second dated observation; (2) no source affirmatively states 'Beebe did not evacuate' — sheltering is inferred from continuous operation plus the absence of any evacuation report, and the CSV's parenthetical claim of 'contemporaneous state roundups' showing no Delaware hospital evacuation is not backed by any URL in the sources field and I could not locate such a roundup. The Sussex County government's Aug 28, 2011 damage assessment confirms the county came through with mostly minor damage but makes no reference to hospitals, so it does not add facility-level support. I searched for any later Irene-aftermath evacuation or closure of Beebe and found none. Recommend the authors either cite a second source or explicitly flag this as single-source.

observed_through_basis: https://www.nyc.gov/html/om/html/2011b/pr311-11_alt.html — "Thankfully they didn't have to use those" (Mayor Bloomberg, PR-311-11, Aug 28, 2011, referring to the backup emergency generators at Bellevue and Coler-Goldwater; i.e. Bellevue rode out Irene on normal power).
notes: The cited DNAinfo URL is live and does say what the abstraction claims — NYU Langone posted a sign redirecting ER patients to Bellevue, 'situated on higher ground just a few blocks south.' Its limitation is timing: it is dated Aug 27, 2011, BEFORE Irene reached New York City early on Aug 28, so on its own it establishes only that Bellevue was open and absorbing diverted patients on the eve of the storm, not that it operated through it. I therefore added two post-landfall/retrospective anchors. Mayor Bloomberg's PR-311-11 of Aug 28, 2011 discusses Bellevue's generator redundancy and states the city's hospitals 'didn't have to use those' backup systems during Irene, which places Bellevue on utility power after the storm passed. ProPublica's retrospective identifies the NYC hospitals that actually emptied for Irene — NYU Langone transferred or discharged all but a few critically ill patients, and 'Coney Island Hospital was also fully evacuated before Irene' — and Bellevue appears in no Irene evacuation list I found, in that piece, in the Columbia Case Consortium Irene case study, in Wikipedia's Effects of Hurricane Irene in New York, or in any 2011 news item. Bellevue sat outside the 2011 Zone A evacuation footprint, which is why it was the designated receiving site. I actively searched for a later forced evacuation or closure during Irene's aftermath and found none; every Bellevue evacuation account in the literature belongs to Superstorm Sandy, Oct 31-Nov 3, 2012, a different storm year, which the CSV detail already correctly distinguishes. Residual weakness for the authors: no source states in so many words that Bellevue was operating with inpatients on Aug 28-29, 2011 — the post-landfall support is convergent and inferential (higher-ground receiving site + generators unused + absent from all evacuee lists) rather than a single direct statement.

The single cited CNN URL is live-blocked (HTTP 451) and was recovered from the Wayback Machine (snapshots 20120118043721 and the 2011 crawl of the same article). The archived article text was extracted in full and searched: it contains NO occurrence of 'Morehead City' in a hospital context, NO occurrence of 'generator', and NO occurrence of 'hospital' in the North Carolina section. Its only Carteret content is 'Carteret County also issued a mandatory evacuation order for visitors in part of the county.' The article is also dated August 25, 2011 - two days BEFORE the Aug 27 Cape Lookout landfall - and is framed entirely as pre-storm preparations, so it could not establish during-storm or post-storm operation even if the hospital were named. Caveat: the archived article is paginated (pages 2-7); pages 2-7 are not held by the Internet Archive (all return Wayback error pages), so a small residual chance remains that the generator sentence sat on an unarchived page. I also checked the adjacent CNN Irene articles that WOULD cover during-storm conditions - the Aug 27 'irene.state.by.state' piece (archived 20110828), the Aug 26 'hurricane.irene.events' live file, and the Aug 26 'irene.preparations' piece - and none mentions a Morehead City hospital or hospital generators; the only NC-hospital-adjacent content is a Sentara Norfolk General lockdown (Virginia). Independent searching (news, NC DPS, NWS MHX event review, NHC TCR, Carteret County News-Times/carolinacoastonline, WUNC, NPR, hospital site, Wikipedia) produced no contemporaneous source placing Carteret General Hospital in operation, on generators, or non-evacuated during Irene. No evidence of a later forced evacuation or closure was found either, so the SIP_OK label is not contradicted - it is simply unsupported. The row's own detail text concedes the facility name is inferred from geography (LOW confidence); this audit finds the underlying generator claim is not present in the cited source at all, so the inference has no documented antecedent. Recommend dropping the event or reclassifying it as unknown/undocumented rather than carrying it as SIP_OK in a peer-reviewed count.

observed_through_basis: https://www.utmb.edu/impact/home/2017/10/02/stopping-for-no-storm-utmb-continues-vital-mission-throughout-hurricane-harvey-historic-rainfall - "As UTMB returned to normal operations on Sept. 1"
notes: Both cited sources fetched live. AMN (Aug 29, 2017) directly supports the abstraction's wording - hospital and ED open, clinics closed. KFDM (Aug 31, 2017) is corroborating rather than direct: it documents Baptist Beaumont's forced evacuation and quotes a Baptist spokeswoman naming UTMB Galveston as a receiving partner, which shows UTMB was functioning and accepting transfers on Aug 31 - i.e., the opposite of being evacuated itself. observed_through_basis: https://www.bpr.org/bpr-news/2024-12-09/mission-health-is-back-on-city-water-after-using-water-tankers-wells-in-helene-aftermath — "no longer trucking in water or relying on well water" (BPR, Dec 9, 2024; article states hospital remained open throughout, with ~14M gallons trucked/welled and 200,000+ gallons/day). Federal corroboration: ASPR TRACIE interview with Mission COO (PDF, 2025): "We did not evacuate."; ED never closed; without municipal water for 54 days.
notes: All five cited URLs fetched directly. Shelter-in-place is unambiguously supported: Mission Hospital (Level II trauma, ~800 inpatients) did not evacuate before or during landfall (Sept 27), the ED never closed, and it operated continuously through total municipal water loss until rejoining city water (BPR Dec 9, 2024; TRACIE: 54 days without municipal water). The reason for 'review' rather than 'keep' is a definitional question the authors must settle, not a source failure: on Oct 7-8, 2024 (11 days post-landfall) HCA announced it would 'temporarily relocate selected stable patients from Mission Hospital to hospitals outside the area hardest hit', with fewer than 100 patients affected across Mission Hospital, Asheville Specialty Hospital (LTACH, St. Joseph's campus, all 12 patients moved) and CarePartners Inpatient Rehabilitation (50+ patients; facility temporarily closed), coordinated through the NC state patient coordination team, explicitly because of the lack of municipal water (WLOS Oct 8; Asheville Watchdog Oct 14, quoting HCA: "This is temporary and routine patient movement"). Mission's main campus never closed, its ERs stayed open, and it resumed accepting inbound transfers within days (TRACIE). The row's detail already discloses this ('a limited number of patients were transferred... in early October'), so the record is internally honest. However, a post-landfall, utility-loss-driven outbound transfer of low-acuity inpatients is what many evacuation taxonomies call a 'partial evacuation' or 'decompression'; whether it counts as 'forced patient movement' depends on the paper's coding rule. If the rule excludes voluntary/precautionary decompression that leaves the hospital open, 'keep' (possibly keep_lower_confidence) is defensible; if any storm-driven outbound inpatient transfer counts, relabel to the partial-evacuation category. Note also that Asheville Specialty Hospital (a separate LTACH under Mission Health, likely its own CCN) was permanently closed after these transfers (NC Health News, Nov 30, 2024) — check it is not conflated with CCN 340002. Minor detail-field discrepancies: tanker count is reported as ~40 (WLOS Oct 4) vs. two rotating trucks (TRACIE) vs. row's '36+'; daily volume 200,000+ gal/day (BPR, NBC) vs. 300,000 (TRACIE); 'two wells' per BPR while TRACIE describes one 900-ft well and Watchdog a FEMA-assisted 750-ft well; '400+ relief nurses' not found verbatim (WLOS Oct 4: 300+ extra personnel; Healthcare Dive: 100+ bussed from Tennessee). None of these affect the SIP_OK label.

No source anywhere states or implies that Blue Ridge Regional evacuated or transferred patients out under duress. One residual limitation: no source explicitly narrates a pre-event decision NOT to evacuate — Helene's WNC impact was inland flooding without a pre-landfall hospital evacuation decision window — so the SIP_OK label rests on continuous documented operation rather than on an explicit 'we chose to shelter' statement. observed_through_basis: https://www.tgh.org/news/tgh-press-releases/2023/august/tampa-general-hospital-remains-safe-and-open-through-hurricane-idalia — "remained on site through the hurricane to care for patients" (verified verbatim in page HTML; press release dated Aug. 30, 2023, the day of Idalia's Big Bend landfall, and titled 'Tampa General Hospital Remains Safe and Open Through Hurricane Idalia')

hospital: NCH Baker Hospital Downtown (Naples Community Hospital)

Important distinction the abstraction gets right and that a reader could easily get wrong: the 450+ people moved to the 4th/5th floors were sheltering employee family members and patient family members, NOT patients, and they were moved WITHIN the building. On its own this source shows staff and the CEO on site during the eyewall passage but does not state whether the hospital kept operating or moved patients, so it is scored 'partial'. I could not locate the underlying Naples Daily News article (repeated Wayback CDX queries for naplesnews.com September 2017 timed out or returned no matching URL, and the WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted). I instead recovered a primary-source substitute from the Wayback Machine: NCH Healthcare System's own weekly 'Straight Talk' message from President and CEO Allen Weiss, MD, dated Sep 14, 2017, verified verbatim: 'NCH never closes due to the dedication, passion, perseverance, and competence of our team comprised of 4,300 colleagues, 800 Medical Staff, and 1,200 volunteers. Hurricane Irma tested our resolve as the eye of the storm passed over both hospitals. Our folks came through yet again caring for about 380 in-patients ranging from Neonates to Rehab and everyone in-between at both hospitals and four Emergency Departments... We also sheltered over 1,200 family members with safe lodging and served 9,000 meals.' (1) The CEO statement is system-level ('both hospitals'), covering Baker Downtown and North Naples together, rather than a Baker-Downtown-specific attestation; it is a self-report by the operator, though it is contemporaneous, specific, and consistent with the independent Naples Daily News-sourced account. Contradiction search: I found no report of any later forced evacuation, closure, or patient transfer out of NCH Baker Hospital Downtown during Irma's aftermath; the Irma hospital casualties in Florida reported in the sources reviewed were elsewhere (e.g., Fishermen's Community Hospital in Marathon, and the Hollywood Hills nursing home). Label stands; MEDIUM confidence remains appropriate given the reliance on an operator statement for the operating-status half of the claim.
